ideas.risks: Minimax equality may fail for infinite law classes or noncompact strategy spaces; measurability of policies over continuous price histories is the main technical point.
ideas.summary: Prove the solver's exact characterization first for a finite class and finite quote grid: show that inf_A sup_theta regret equals sup_pi Psi_T,K(pi), where the Bayes learner maximizes the posterior predictive grid reward at each time.
ideas.title: Finite-Grid Minimax Identity
ideas.why_promising: This is the load-bearing claim in the solver attempt. If it is true, the right characterization is predictability/value rather than a tail condition.

ideas.risks: If the protocol contains unmodeled feedback beyond public prices, or if actions can affect observations, the myopic argument breaks.
ideas.summary: Check carefully that, under exogenous public prices, the Bayes-optimal policy for a fixed prior is pointwise myopic: at time t choose a maximizing a for E[r_t(a) | P_1:t], because actions do not affect future prices or information.
ideas.title: Bayes Myopic Optimality
ideas.why_promising: It justifies the posterior predictive term in Psi_T(pi). A small conditioning error here would invalidate the proposed exact formula.

ideas.risks: Strict inequality P > a and atoms can cause nonattainment; conditional suprema may be nonmeasurable without epsilon-selectors.
ideas.summary: Pass from finite quote grids to [0,1] using downward rounding. Quantify whether the minimax value and sup_pi Psi differ from their K-grid versions by at most O(T/K), and handle a=1 and nonattainment with suprema.
ideas.title: Continuum Action Limit
ideas.why_promising: The original problem has continuum quotes, and previous notes repeatedly found max-vs-sup issues. This turns the clean finite theorem into a theorem for the stated model.

ideas.risks: This may seem semantic, but it affects the exact iff statement: regret against a fixed comparator can be negative when adaptive policies beat every fixed quote.
ideas.summary: Clarify the sign convention in the characterization. Determine whether sublinear learnability means inf_A sup_theta R_T^theta(A) = o(T), positive part o(T), or only an upper bound R_T <= o(T), and test singleton laws where the adaptive Bayes reward exceeds the fixed-comparator value by Theta(T).
ideas.title: Positive-Part Convention
ideas.why_promising: The solver already notes Psi_T(pi) can be negative. The final theorem must not assert a false equality or necessity because of negative regret values.

ideas.risks: The optimization may collapse to weak one-block bounds, or become essentially as hard as computing the minimax value itself.
ideas.summary: Use the exact Bayes-gap functional as a variational problem under a tail envelope such as beta(h) <= B(h) or delta_T(H) <= T B(H). Try to maximize sup_pi Psi_T(pi) and compare the resulting lower rate to the truncation upper rate.
ideas.title: Tail-Constrained Bayes Gap
ideas.why_promising: This directly attacks the missing matching lower bound for power tails without relying on the already-refuted one-block heuristic.

ideas.risks: Independent blocks may average out under the fixed expected comparator; a global hidden type may be learned after the first reveal; tails may violate the intended envelope.
ideas.summary: Design multi-scale or limited-leakage priors that accumulate Bayes gap across many unresolved delayed rewards. Candidate designs include hierarchical hidden states, separated quote intervals, or terminal observations with small TV/KL so each reveal gives limited information.
ideas.title: Multi-Scale Lower Bound
ideas.why_promising: The q-scaled hidden-terminal atom is valid but too weak for power-tail rate matching. A controlled accumulation mechanism is the main missing lower-bound ingredient.

ideas.risks: If phrased only as known singleton laws, these examples are already explained by the oracle lemma and may not add new minimax insight.
ideas.summary: Formalize the rare-history and tiny-value long-delay examples. Compute beta, Delta, delta, and Psi for each, and decide whether they separate essential-sup tails from average/value-sensitive criteria in a nontrivial unknown-class setting.
ideas.title: Raw-Tail Separation Examples
ideas.why_promising: These examples can prevent future false necessity claims and clarify exactly what information raw beta throws away.

ideas.risks: The resulting object may be tautological rather than a clean scalar condition, and may not simplify rate statements.
ideas.summary: Relate the truncation upper theorem to the Bayes-gap characterization. Prove weak duality bounds like sup_pi Psi_T(pi) <= C sqrt(T H log K) + T/K + sup_theta delta_T^theta(H), and look for a posterior-truncation loss that is closer to necessary and sufficient.
ideas.title: Dualize The Upper Bound
ideas.why_promising: It would connect the practical sufficient condition to the proposed exact characterization and may reveal the right effective-delay quantity.

ideas.risks: This is a separate regime from the finite-horizon minimax theorem, and standard doubling-style methods might defeat naive lower bounds.
ideas.summary: Investigate the horizon-free known-law regime. Formalize or refute the two-deadline super-growing deterministic construction showing that the horizon-aware oracle does not imply one anytime policy with sublinear regret at all horizons.
ideas.title: Anytime Boundary Case
ideas.why_promising: It sharpens the model taxonomy and prevents overextending the known-law oracle lemma.

ideas.risks: May be outside the intended problem if prices are meant to be exogenous; causal regret definitions can become ambiguous quickly.
ideas.summary: Audit the action-dependent price setting separately. Define whether comparator rewards are evaluated on learner-induced or comparator-induced paths, then construct a minimal example showing why the delayed full-information reduction fails without exogeneity.
ideas.title: Action-Dependent Markets
ideas.why_promising: The upper theorem and Bayes-gap formula both rely on fixed counterfactual rewards. If the protocol allows action-dependent prices, the main theorem must explicitly exclude or replace that model.
